title: Linear decrease in VO2max and performance with increasing altitude in endurance athletes
population: 8 endurance-trained athletes, hypobaric chamber simulating 300-2,800 m
findings: VO2max fell linearly from 66 +/- 1.6 mL/kg/min at 300 m to 55 +/- 1.6 at 2,800 m, a 6.3% decrease per 1,000 m (range 4.6-7.5%).
Time to exhaustion at a constant velocity (associated with 107% of sea-level VO2max) decreased 14.5% per 1,000 m between 300 and 2,800 m (P < 0.001).
Both VO2max and performance already decreased from 300 to 800 m (P < 0.01; P < 0.05).
Arterial O2 saturation at test cessation fell from 89.0 +/- 2.9% at 300 m to 76.5 +/- 4.0% at 2,800 m.
limitations: Eight endurance-trained athletes, acute exposure in a hypobaric chamber (simulated altitude), time to exhaustion at a fixed supramaximal speed rather than race pace. No acclimatisation.
implications: For acute exposure, expect maximal aerobic capacity to fall about 6% per 1,000 m (range 4.6-7.5%) from near sea level; scale altitude-course effort expectations from this, not pace directly: the abstract reports VO2max and time to exhaustion, not race pace.
Label altitude adjustments approximate: individuals vary and acclimatisation is not modelled.

verification.notes: Crossref: Eur J Appl Physiol 96(4):404-412, print 2006 (online 2005-11-26), two authors match (Hallen with diacritic). PubMed PMID 16311764 abstract supports all numbers. Added the 107% VO2max test speed; removed direct VO2max-to-pace scaling.
